review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about the patch's necessity due to the prevalence of PREEMPT_NONE kernels and suggested a simpler backporting approach.

> >  		spin_unlock(ptl);
> >  		if (pageout)
> >  			reclaim_pages(&folio_list);
> > +		cond_resched();
> >  		return 0;
> >  	}
> > 
> 
> This same improvement came naturally from refactoring the entire
> function into a proper pagewalk structure:
> 
> https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20260922235830.2350770-10-gourry@gourry.net/

I'm thinking

Fixes: 9c276cc65a58 ("mm: introduce MADV_COLD")

Sep 25 2019.  So 5.x and 6.x kernels want this.  Current kernels
actually don't need this because PREEMPT_NONE has virtually
disappeared.  But 99%(?) of machines run 5.x and 6.x.

I'll go with Wei's simple one-liner for backportability & safety. 
Let's look at broader changes in future -rc cycles.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page allocation mechanism in Linux to make defragmentation mode retries follow the promoted order of requests, rather than the original request order. This change aims to prevent indefinite retrying by order-0 requests and reduce memory pressure caused by frequent direct reclaim runs. The promoted order is computed once per iteration and passed to relevant functions, ensuring consistency across different callers. Additionally, the patch resets retry counters when a promoted request takes the fallback path, allowing for a full retry budget before OOM killing is considered.

series_items.subject: [PATCH for-7.5 1/5] memcg: move memory.high enforcement out of try_charge_memcg()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the code in try_charge_memcg() by moving memory.high enforcement into a new function called memcg_enforce_high(). This change makes the code easier to read and maintain, while also allowing for more flexibility in handling high memory usage. The new function checks if the current or any of its ancestors are over their respective memory.high limits and takes action accordingly, such as scheduling reclaim or slowing down the task. No functional changes were made.

series_items.subject: [PATCH for-7.5 2/5] memcg: use high_work for kernel threads
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the memory cgroup (memcg) handling for kernel threads, treating them similarly to interrupts. It introduces a new condition to determine whether a worker should be used for reclaim and throttling during a charge, skipping these operations if a kernel thread is involved. The change affects how kernel threads handle memory.high reclamation and throttling, allowing them to skip these tasks and instead rely on workers to manage memory usage.

series_items.subject: [PATCH for-7.5 3/5] memcg: use high_work for remote charges
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the memcg (memory cgroup) handling of high memory usage to use a worker thread for remote charges, which are charges that go to a cgroup outside the current task's cgroup and its ancestors. This change is necessary because the high handler currently uses the current task's mm, which cannot handle these overages. The patch adds a check using mm_match_cgroup() before checking the high limits, and if it does not match, it uses the worker thread instead of recording task overage or doing synchronous reclaim and throttling. This change ensures that remote charges are handled correctly and efficiently.

series_items.subject: [PATCH for-7.5 4/5] memcg: avoid queuing high_work from reclaim
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents the high_work worker from queuing itself during memory reclamation by skipping memory.high enforcement for tasks that would use high_work and have PF_MEMALLOC set, thus avoiding infinite recursion.

series_items.subject: [PATCH for-7.5 5/5] memcg: simplify high limit handling after a charge
series_items.patch_summary: This patch simplifies the handling of high limits in memory cgroups by separating the hierarchy scan from high-limit enforcement. It introduces a new variable to track whether the task is running in user context, and uses this information to determine whether to queue high_work or record the task's overage after scanning the hierarchy. The patch also clarifies comments and removes redundant code, but does not introduce any functional changes.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series cleans up the enforcement of memory.high limits in Linux, specifically for kernel threads and remote charges. The changes move the high limit enforcement into a separate function, use a worker to handle reclamation, and add a guard to prevent infinite loops when reclaiming from its own memory usage. The patches also simplify the handling of high limits after a charge and remove unnecessary checks. The goal is to improve performance by reducing delays caused by reclaiming and sleeping during charges.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] sched/psi: Remove the RCU wait from trigger destruction

version_history.subject: [PATCH] sched/psi: Remove the RCU wait from trigger destruction

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch removes the RCU (Read-Copy Update) wait from the destruction of PSI (Pressure Stall Information) triggers in the Linux kernel. The RCU wait was introduced to protect worker and trigger lookups, but it has become unnecessary due to changes made in subsequent commits. The patch replaces the RCU wait with a simple NULL check using rcu_access_pointer(), which is sufficient for the current implementation. This change improves performance by reducing lock contention and making the code more efficient.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/2] mm: zswap: use separate compression and decompression requests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the compression and decompression requests in the zswap module, allowing them to run independently and reducing contention between high-priority loads and low-priority stores. This change improves performance by eliminating the need for a single per-CPU buffer and mutex, which could lead to long wait times when other tasks are runnable. The patch also simplifies the code by removing unnecessary checks and freeing resources correctly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/2] mm: zswap: use stack requests for synchronous decompression
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the performance of synchronous decompression in zswap by allowing some algorithms to use stack requests instead of heap requests. This reduces contention on a per-CPU mutex, which can lead to stalls for higher-priority loads. The change is made possible because the codecs keep their own stream locks and the per-CPU context is set up before its CPU comes online. The patch adds a function to check whether an algorithm can use stack requests and applies it to software compressors. This results in a smaller load path, but also increases the memory usage by 216 bytes for each load.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch series aims to reduce contention on loads in the zswap compression algorithm by introducing separate requests and mutexes for compression and decompression, allowing loads to run concurrently without waiting for stores.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch series but expressed concerns about understanding its implications.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Oct 9, 2026 at 6:31 PM Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev> wrote:
>
> Stores and loads serialize on the same per-CPU acomp request and mutex.
> A low-priority store can be preempted as soon as the compressor drops
> its stream lock, while it still holds the mutex. A higher-priority load
> on that CPU then waits until the store runs again, which can take a
> long time when other tasks are runnable.
>
> Give compression and decompression their own request, completion wait
> and mutex. Since commit e2c3b6b21c77f ("mm: zswap: use SG list
> decompression APIs from zsmalloc"), the per-CPU buffer is only used for
> compression, so group it with the compression request. Independent
> requests can share the per-CPU transform; the codecs and drivers
> synchronize their shared state internally. Loads can still wait for
> each other on the decompression mutex, and stores still serialize on
> the compression mutex.
>
> acomp_request_free() ignores NULL requests, so drop the check in
> acomp_ctx_free().
>
> This follows the proposal from Sergey Senozhatsky for the same split
> for zram [1].
>
> [1] https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261005122036.718976-10-senozhatsky@chromium.org/
>
> Signed-off-by: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>

Acked-by: Nhat Pham <nphamcs@gmail.com>
